subject: Clarifying billing floor, rounding quantum, and SKU mapping
messages:

Subject: Billing question: rounding / streaming / 32k context billing

Hi Stephanie,

Thanks for the demo yesterday — the team liked the latency and the context handling. A few hands-on questions came up from finance and engineering about how we'll actually be billed so we can model costs for the POC. Short list: 

1) If we stream responses, are partial streamed tokens billed immediately or aggregated into a per-session window?
2) We will use the 32k context model for multi-doc retrieval + summarization. Does Redwood bill on the actual context length used per call or by a fixed chunking band (e.g., 8k vs 32k SKU)?
3) Rounding / minimums: what is the quantum (smallest billable unit) and how do you round for short calls (e.g., single-shot classification requests of 30 tokens)? Any examples with math would help.

Procurement also asked whether we can map a subscription SKU (seats + token bundle) to a pilot with a lower minimum. We're trying to produce an expense forecast for Q4.

Appreciate a short worked example and any invoice sample you can share.

Best,
Emma
Emma Zhao
Director, AI Platforms | Acme Retail

Subject: Re: Billing question: rounding / streaming / 32k context billing

Hi Emma — thanks for the clear list. Short answers up front, then a short worked example and next steps.

1) Streaming: we bill on the final token footprint for the request after the server-side aggregation window (default 5s). For long streams we commit tokens in rolling windows to keep memory low; if a client keeps an open stream longer than the window we charge in additional quanta as those windows complete.

2) Context/Model SKU: billing is by actual tokens processed (input + output) and the model SKU sets performance/latency and the max sequence length. There is also an optional "context band" billing mode for customers who prefer fixed SKU pricing (e.g., a 32k SKU priced differently than 8k SKU). For your standard usage we recommend metered-by-token (actual tokens) to avoid overpaying for unused context.

3) Quantum & rounding: our public default quantum is 50 tokens. For example calls below we show how we round and how minimums apply. We can offer a pilot-specific quantum/minimum per contract.

Worked example (short):
- Call A: single-shot classification. Input: 18 tokens. Output: 12 tokens. Raw total = 30 tokens.
- Rounding: 30 rounds up to the nearest quantum (50) => billed as 50 tokens.
- Call B: streaming response that emits 220 tokens over 40s. We commit 5s windows; that maps to 5 rolling windows of ~44 tokens each. Each 44 token window rounds to 50 => 5 * 50 = 250 tokens billed.
- Context-heavy call: ingest 18k tokens (for summarization) + output 1k => 19k billed. For your 32k model the token count is exact; there's no forced jump to 32k unless you elect context-band pricing.

Pilot concession options we typically use:
- Lower quantum for pilot (25 token quantum, min 50) for the first 90 days.
- Or keep 50 token quantum but apply a pilot rebate credit on the invoice equal to 15% of billed tokens (applied post-invoice) to ease forecasting.

I've attached a sample invoice mapping (acme_sample_invoice.csv) and our internal playbook that explains quantum examples (redwood_billing_playbook.pdf).

Next steps: Marcus — can you confirm whether the finance team needs a guaranteed per-call floor in the agreement or if a post-invoice rebate is sufficient? Priyom — if we set a pilot quantum to 25 tokens, does that need a change in how we meter or just a contract-level override?

Emma — if that aligns, I'll send a short SOW + pilot terms and include a sample DocuSign for procurement.

Thanks,
Stephanie Nguyen
Principal Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference

From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Billing question: rounding / streaming / 32k context billing

Stephanie / Priyom — quick internal note. Finance will often push for a per-call floor to make forecasting deterministic; I prefer giving the rebate instead (less operational friction). Operational notes:

- Metering: switching quantum from 50 -> 25 is a billing-config toggle; runtime emits raw token counts and billing merges by window. No code changes required, just a ratecard override on the account.
- For streaming, the 5s commit window we use today is configurable per-customer; for predictable cost we can set the window to 10s for this account (fewer windows for long streams) but that increases tail latency exposure on aborts — tradeoff to mention.
- Concession recommendation for ACME pilot:
  * 25-token quantum for first 90 days, min per-request floor 50 tokens OR
  * Keep 50-token quantum, but 12% fixed pilot rebate applied monthly (easier for procurement).

I can sign off on the 25-token pilot quantum + 10% discount on list pricing for 3 months if Stephanie gets verbal approval from Emma/procurement. If procurement insists on guaranteed floor for each call we should map that as a contract term (adds legal).

-Marcus

Hi Emma / procurement team — following our internal review we've outlined two pilot options so your FP&A can model both. We prefer Option A (pilot quantum) but leaving both for you to choose.

Option A (recommended for engineering predictability):
- Pilot duration: 90 days starting on activation.
- Quantum: 25 tokens.
- Per-call floor: 50 tokens (any call rounds up to nearest 25, minimum billed 50).
- Discount: 10% off list for the pilot period.
- Streaming window: default 5s commit; can change to 10s on request for fewer billing windows.

Option B (procurement-friendly):
- Quantum: 50 tokens (standard).
- No per-call floor beyond quantum.
- Monthly pilot rebate: 12% of billed tokens credited on the following invoice.

Attached: acme_sample_invoice.csv (mock invoice showing sample calls mapped to billed tokens) and redwood_billing_playbook.pdf (explanations and edge-case examples). DocuSign SOW link: https://docusign.example.com/envelope/ABCD1234

Please reply with which option procurement prefers and we will prepare an SOW. If you'd like, I can lock in Option A verbally while legal drafts the short amendment.

Thanks again — appreciate the quick turnaround.
